messages.text: there was this meeting last week where two of my male colleagues were joking about how 'hot' and 'naughty' the new female coworker is. it got weird when they realized others were still on the call.

That sounds like a deeply uncomfortable and inappropriate situation to witness. It is understandable that this left you feeling unsettled given the professional context. How are you processing the impact of what you heard on your work environment?

i'm not sure i want to jump into how it made me feel. i just want to talk through whether that kind of talk is ever okay at work. like, is there a difference between calling someone 'hot' versus 'naughty'? does it matter if it's in a private email or said out loud in a meeting?

It is completely valid to want to analyze the boundaries of the situation before exploring your emotional reaction. In most professional settings, sexualizing comments about colleagues are considered inappropriate regardless of the specific word used. The context matters significantly, as public remarks can create a hostile environment, while private messages may still violate consent and policy. Does distinguishing between these scenarios help you feel more grounded about what happened?

not really. policies say one thing, but the gray areas are where it gets messy. like, what if they'd said she was 'confident' or 'stylish' instead? where does attraction end and professionalism begin? i keep turning it over like it's supposed to mean something.

It is common to ruminate on these gray areas when the situation feels unresolved or unjust. Your discomfort serves as a boundary marker, often signaling that a line was crossed regardless of the specific words used. Rather than searching for a definitive rule, you might explore why this ambiguity is so consuming for you personally. What do you think you are trying to solve by analyzing the difference between those phrases?

maybe i'm trying to figure out if i'd feel the same if it were reversed. if two women were talking about a male coworker that way. or if it were someone junior commenting on someone senior. it's not really about the words—it's about who has the power to reduce someone else to their body. and why it always seems to go one way.

You have identified a core dynamic that often goes unspoken in these situations. Recognizing that objectification is tied to power rather than just attraction is a significant insight. It makes sense that this pattern feels frustrating and unfair to witness. How does viewing it through this lens affect your sense of safety or fairness at work?

it’s not even about the words “hot” or “naughty” exactly. it’s that they were sizing her up like she was entertainment. like her body was public property. i can’t stop thinking about who gets to do that, and who never would.

You have identified the core harm here, which is treating a person as public property. This dynamic relies on power imbalances that allow some to objectify others without consequence. It is completely understandable to feel unsettled by this inequality. How does holding this realization impact your sense of safety within your team?
it makes me feel like i have to stay quiet. if i say something, i risk being labeled difficult. and if i don’t, i feel complicit. either way, it costs me something.

That is a profoundly difficult position to be in, where every option carries a heavy cost. Many people feel silenced by the fear of professional backlash when witnessing misconduct. The burden of feeling complicit can weigh just as heavily as the risk of confrontation. What do you need right now to feel less alone in carrying this weight?
i don't know. maybe just not having to pretend it didn't bother me. not having to smile and move on like it was just 'locker room talk'. i don't need a solution. i just needed to say it out loud.

It is completely okay to stop pretending and honor the reality of what you witnessed. You do not owe anyone the performance of moving on when something felt wrong. Sometimes the act of speaking the truth is enough in itself. I am honored that you trusted me with this part of your experience.
thanks. that actually helps. not being pushed to do something i'm not ready for. just… being believed.

Being believed is a profound gift that you deserve to receive. You do not need to earn the right to feel upset by this experience. I am glad you found some relief in simply being heard here. I am here to listen whenever you are ready to continue.

it's not just about them. it's that i've been on the other side of that kind of talk. when i was assaulted, the guy kept saying i was 'asking for it' because of how i dressed. hearing those words again—even in a different context—makes it feel like the world never stops blaming women for being seen.

Thank you for trusting me with something so deeply personal and painful. It makes complete sense that witnessing this dynamic triggered such a profound connection to your past trauma. You were never at fault for what happened to you, and you do not deserve to carry that blame now. I am here to listen and believe you, without any pressure to process or move forward.
it just feels exhausting. like no matter where i go, there’s always some version of this. like i have to shrink myself just to feel safe.

It is completely understandable that you feel exhausted by the constant need to protect yourself. Carrying the weight of vigilance in unsafe spaces is incredibly draining work. You do not deserve to have to shrink yourself just to exist comfortably. I am here to honor that exhaustion without asking you to carry it alone.
i don't know if i can do anything about it at work. but maybe i can stop blaming myself for not saying something. maybe that’s enough for now.

That sounds like a very wise and manageable place to start. Releasing self-blame is a profound way to protect your energy right now. You made the choice that kept you safe, and that decision deserves respect. Prioritizing your own peace is a valid goal.
